title: Scheduled job service
brief: Customers register jobs: "call my web address every night at 02:00" or "every hour on the hour". Aim to fire within 5 seconds; work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed. Retry safely after a crash. One external effect requires the customer endpoint to honor a stable job occurrence key. Half the world picks the top of the hour, so a huge crowd of jobs comes due in the same second.

clarify.q: How late may a job fire?
clarify.a: The webhook p99 target is 5,000 ms. Work still waiting after 60 seconds counts as failed, even if it eventually runs.

clarify.q: What if a job is delivered twice?
clarify.a: That is the worst outcome: a bill sent twice, a backup run twice. Twice must never happen, even if a worker crashes and the job is tried again.

clarify.q: Do jobs we cannot run get lost?
clarify.a: No. A job that keeps failing is parked where the customer can see it, and everything else carries on.

notes: A job record is about 1 KB (approx.).
At the top of the hour about 1,200 requests a second come due for a few minutes (approx.).
One app server handles about 1,000 requests a second (approx.).

Customer web addresses have an aggregate quota of 10,000 webhooks/s across independent endpoints, with no per-call infrastructure fee. One endpoint can still time out. External one-effect delivery requires endpoint idempotency or reconciliation.

numbers.label: Jobs firing per second at the top of the hour
Job records stored
numbers.how: 40 million jobs × 1 KB ≈ 40 GB, small enough for one database (approx.)

numbers.label: Workers to run the top of the hour
numbers.how: Each worker finishes about 200 light jobs a second; 840 ÷ 200 ≈ 5, plus room for retries and the 3 times crowd (approx.)

hints: Jobs come due in a wall at the top of the hour. What can hold the wall so the servers are not flooded?
A queue holds the wall and workers drain it at their own pace. If a worker dies, the same job is tried again, so something must notice a job already ran.
Load balancer, servers, a queue with workers, an idempotency store, a dead-letter queue for jobs that keep failing, and a SQL database.

editorial.summary: The schedule tells the system what is due. A queue turns the wall of due jobs into a steady line, workers pull from it at a fixed pace, and an idempotency store makes a retried job a no-op. Jobs that keep failing are parked so one bad job never blocks the rest.

designs.name: Queue, workers and an idempotency store
designs.why: The servers drop each due job on the queue, and the workers drain it. The worker durably claims a job occurrence and reuses its key at the customer endpoint. After an unknown outcome it reconciles with that endpoint; a local lookup alone cannot prevent a second external effect. A dead-letter queue parks jobs that keep failing, and the SQL database holds the schedule.

tradeoffs: Firing a few seconds early and spreading the wall over a short window flattens the peak, at the price of jobs that are not to the second.
A local lookup alone cannot guarantee one external effect after a crash. Use the same job occurrence key at a cooperating endpoint, or expose the unknown outcome for reconciliation.
A dead-letter queue keeps a poison job from blocking the line, but someone must look at what lands there.
One database is simple and enough for the schedule; sharding it by customer is the next step if jobs reach billions.
editorial.realWorld: Hosted schedulers fire millions of jobs a day, and the top of the hour is always the busiest minute, since people pick round times (approx.).

third-party-api.description: Independent customer endpoints, reached with a stable key for each scheduled occurrence.

correctness.prompt: Scheduled job service: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.
